subtype: Approach: anticipating questions with a friend [Action]
passage: Sahil booked the small meeting room in the hostel for Saturday evening. Madhav had agreed to play the tough examiner and had brought a list of questions written on the back of an old timetable. "Why this dataset and not a larger one?" "How do you know the result is not by chance?" "What would you do with more time?" Five in all. After each one, Sahil wrote an answer in a couple of lines. Two questions were easy. Two took a while to answer well. One, about the method's limits, could not be answered at all. Sahil marked it in red and put it on Sunday's reading list. They ended with tea, and Madhav gave a sober thumbs up.

qa.q: How many questions did Madhav ask?
qa.a: Madhav asked five questions in all.

qa.q: What was Sahil probably feeling when the question on the method's limits could not be answered?
qa.a: Sahil probably felt a bit uneasy but honest, since the question was marked in red and put on the reading list.

qa.q: What other approach could help Sahil practise, and why?
qa.a: Sahil could also answer the questions aloud to a phone recorder, because hearing the answers shows which sound unclear.

qa.q: How might Madhav see the role of tough examiner?
qa.a: Madhav is helping Sahil find weak spots early, and probably feels useful while doing it.

grounding: A listener acts as a tough examiner and asks five questions, and the student writes short answers and notes what needs more reading.

subtype: Approach: anticipating questions with a friend [Action]
passage:
'Okay, I'm the external examiner. I'm grumpy and I skipped breakfast,' Pooja said, folding her arms. 'Question one. Why did you choose only two hospitals?'
Lokesh cleared his throat. 'Time and access. Two gave us permission.'
'Hm. Question two. How do you know the nurses answered honestly?'
'The survey was anonymous.' He scribbled the answer on his notepad.
'Three. What would change with ten hospitals?'
'Um...' He stopped. 'I don't know. More variety?'
'That's weak.'
'I know.' He wrote 'Q3 – read about sample size' and circled it.
Question four was about his graph's scale; he answered fine. Five, about costs, stumped him again. Another circle.
'Five questions, two circles,' Pooja said, unfolding her arms. 'Better than I expected.'
'Library tonight, then. For the circles.'

qa.q: Why did Lokesh choose only two hospitals?
qa.a: Time and access. Two gave us permission.

qa.q: How did Lokesh feel when he couldn't answer question three?
qa.a: He felt stuck and a little embarrassed, admitting it was weak, but calm enough to note it for more reading.

qa.q: What else could Lokesh do with the circled questions?
qa.a: Read up on them tonight and try the answers aloud to Pooja again tomorrow.

qa.q: How does playing the examiner feel for Pooja?
qa.a: Pooja enjoys being grumpy and tough, and is pleasantly surprised that only two questions stumped Lokesh.

grounding: Shows a friend playing a tough examiner with five questions while the student writes short answers and marks the ones needing more reading.

subtype: Approach: anticipating questions with a friend [Action]
passage:
Three days before my thesis defence, I asked my friend Ramesh to be as mean as possible. I'm Farhan, and I'd heard the panel liked to grill people.
We sat in the empty seminar room. Ramesh took the professors' chair and fired five questions at me. Why this method and not another? What's the biggest weakness in your data? How would you explain this to a farmer? What if the rainfall pattern changes? What would you do with another year?
I answered out loud and wrote each answer in two or three lines on a card. Three came out fine. Two, the weakness and the rainfall question, came out as mumbling. I starred those and spent the next two evenings reading.
At the defence, the panel asked the weakness question almost word for word. I looked at the professor and gave my three lines, calmly. I nearly laughed. Ramesh had been meaner.

qa.q: Which two questions came out as mumbling?
qa.a: The weakness and the rainfall question.

qa.q: How did Farhan feel when the panel asked the weakness question?
qa.a: Farhan felt calm and even amused, nearly laughing, because the answer had been prepared.

qa.q: What else could Farhan do if the panel asks something not on the cards?
qa.a: Pause, say what is known and what would need checking, instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel hearing the defence went well?
qa.a: Ramesh would likely feel proud that being mean in practice helped Farhan stay calm.

grounding: Shows a friend acting as a tough examiner with five questions, and the student writing short answers and reading more on the weak ones.
